claim: A failure detector for vision-language-action robot policies that reads only the policy's own internal action representations, and is trained only on whole-episode success or failure labels with no per-step annotation, can flag impending task failure during execution more reliably than existing runtime detectors, including on tasks it never saw in training. Detectors are compared at thresholds calibrated on held-out successful episodes so that the false-alarm rate on successful runs is bounded at a chosen level. Supported only if, on held-out tasks, it has the highest class-balanced accuracy and the highest time-weighted accuracy (which also rewards early alarms) of every compared detector, for every policy and benchmark tested, including at least one autoregressive and one flow-matching policy and a physical robot; and if it is more accurate than a vision-language-model monitor that watches the camera stream, while being fast enough to run at every control step.

experiments: Collect rollouts and fix the splits. Setup: run released fine-tuned checkpoints of an autoregressive policy (OpenVLA) and a flow-matching policy (pi0) on the ten long-horizon LIBERO-10 tasks, and a second flow-matching policy (pi0.5) on ten VLABench tasks. In each benchmark hold out three of the ten tasks as unseen, with a different random partition for each of three seeds. Per benchmark: 210 training rollouts, 35 held-out successful rollouts for calibration, 105 evaluation rollouts on seen tasks and 150 on unseen tasks. Label each rollout only as success or failure. Base success rates are 51.0% (OpenVLA), 84.2% (pi0) and 40.3% (pi0.5). Extract a per-step embedding from the policy's action token or action head, averaged across layers for the autoregressive model and taken before the velocity head at the last denoising step for the flow models, then average over non-overlapping windows.

Fix how an alarm is decided and scored, for every method alike. Setup: turn per-step failure scores into alarms with a time-varying threshold built by functional conformal prediction from held-out successful episodes, which bounds the trajectory-level false-alarm rate on successful runs at alpha. Count a failure episode as detected if an alarm fires at any step. Report balanced accuracy, accuracy weighted by class frequency, and time-weighted accuracy, which discounts each true detection by how late in the episode it fires, averaged over alpha in {0.15, 0.20, 0.25} and three seeds. Tune all hyperparameters, for the new detector and for every baseline, only on seen tasks, then apply them unchanged to unseen tasks. For unseen tasks the calibration set comes from seen tasks, since unseen tasks are not available at calibration time.

Compare against every family of existing detector on LIBERO-10. Setup: twelve baselines on the same embeddings and protocol: out-of-distribution detectors (Mahalanobis, cosine k-NN, PCA-KMeans, random network distillation, LogpZO), sampling-based uncertainty with 10 action samples per step (cluster entropy, EigenScore, STAC, ACE), classifiers trained by copying the episode label to every step (SAFE with an LSTM and with an MLP), and for OpenVLA also token-probability entropy and negative log-likelihood. Result: on OpenVLA the new detector reaches balanced accuracy 0.852 on seen and 0.834 on unseen tasks, against 0.823 and 0.775 for the best baseline (SAFE-MLP); on pi0 it reaches 0.885 and 0.892 against 0.870 and 0.801. Time-weighted accuracy is also highest in every cell (OpenVLA unseen 0.663 vs 0.590). The out-of-distribution detectors are competitive on seen tasks but collapse on unseen ones, e.g. Mahalanobis falls from 0.670 to 0.513 on OpenVLA.

Repeat on a second benchmark and policy. Setup: VLABench with pi0.5, same splits, baselines and protocol. Result: balanced accuracy 0.856 on seen and 0.713 on unseen tasks against 0.788 and 0.641 for the strongest classifier baseline; time-weighted accuracy 0.662 and 0.608 against 0.581 and 0.500. Some out-of-distribution baselines come close on unseen tasks (cosine k-NN 0.704 balanced accuracy).

Test on a physical robot with naturally occurring failures. Setup: a UFactory xArm 6 with a RealSense camera, eight tabletop tasks in two suites of four (cube placement and stacking; kitchen objects into a bowl and bowl onto plate), pi0.5 fine-tuned with LoRA on 25 demonstrations per task. Randomise initial robot state and object layout and apply no induced perturbations, giving 98 successes and 62 failures for the cube suite and 102 and 58 for kitchen. Hold out one task per suite as unseen. Sampling-based detectors are excluded because they cannot run in real time. Result: balanced accuracy seen/unseen 0.966/0.914 (cube) and 0.968/0.972 (kitchen), against SAFE-MLP's 0.992/0.797 and 0.784/0.878; time-weighted accuracy is highest in all four settings (cube unseen 0.800 vs 0.650). SAFE-MLP does beat it on seen cube balanced accuracy.

Rule out that the gain comes from training a classifier on the policy's embeddings at all, rather than from avoiding the label noise of copying the episode label to every step. Setup: train the same detector on the same embeddings, windowing and settings, but with the failure label assigned uniformly to every step of a failed episode and a margin loss on all steps. Result: the uniform-label version is 19.4 points worse in balanced accuracy on OpenVLA and 18.6 points worse on pi0 on LIBERO-10. A t-SNE view of the embeddings shows heavy overlap between success and failure steps under uniform labels and clear separation once steps before the annotated onset are relabelled as success.

Compare with a monitor that judges the camera stream directly. Setup: prompt Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with online video question answering over all frames up to the current step, asking for a success or failure judgment at each frame, and call an episode failed if any frame is judged a failure; LIBERO-10 with OpenVLA. Measure balanced accuracy and per-step latency on one A6000 GPU. Result: 0.712 balanced accuracy at 2.343 s per step for the vision-language monitor against 0.843 at 0.001 s for the embedding-based detector.

Check that the result is not an artefact of lucky hyperparameters. Setup: on LIBERO-10 with pi0, sweep both loss margins over {0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}; separately sweep the temporal window size from 1 to 32 for OpenVLA and pi0; and compare MLP, GRU, single-layer Transformer and LSTM backbones on identical inputs and training. Result: balanced accuracy varies by less than 4 points across all margin settings (best 88.8%), moderate windows beat very small ones with the best window matching the policy's action-chunk length for pi0, and all three sequence backbones clearly beat the per-step MLP (OpenVLA 0.765 vs 0.80-0.84).
